stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: Drag the satellite to set its distance $r$ from Earth, use the slider to set its speed $v$, then LAUNCH. Watch how the orbit changes shape as $v$ moves away from $v_{\text{circ}}$.
stages.concept: For a circular orbit, gravity provides the centripetal force: $\dfrac{G M}{r^{2}} = \dfrac{v^{2}}{r}$, hence $v_{\text{circ}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{G M}{r}}$.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: Three dashed target orbits are shown, each labelled with its period $T$. Match each one: pick $r$ to align with the ring, then set $v$ so the preview ring turns solid teal (that is $v = v_{\text{circ}}$).
stages.concept: Kepler's third law: $T^{2} = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}}{G M} \, r^{3}$. The period depends only on the orbit's radius, not on the satellite's mass.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: No preview ring. Only the target periods are given. For each one, compute $r$ from Kepler's third law, set $v = v_{\text{circ}}(r)$, then LAUNCH. You have limited shots — pen and paper first.
stages.concept: $r = \left(\dfrac{G M \, T^{2}}{4\pi^{2}}\right)^{1/3}$, then $v_{\text{circ}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{G M}{r}}$. Use $G M = 4 \cdot 10^{5} \ \text{km}^{3}/\text{s}^{2}$.

labels.tip1: drag the satellite radially, move v, then LAUNCH — v = v_circ closes the orbit
labels.tip2: align the preview ring with a target, then dial v until it turns teal
labels.tip3: compute r from T, then v_circ(r) on paper before you launch
labels.peek_tip_kepler: T² is proportional to r³. Doubling r multiplies T by 2^(3/2) ≈ 2.83 — a small radius change swings the period a lot.
labels.peek_tip_geo: A geostationary orbit has T = 24 h. Any orbit period ≈ 24 h → r ≈ 42 000 km. Use it as a reference anchor.
labels.peek_tip_vcirc: Once you have r, always finish with v = √(μ/r). Skipping this step opens the orbit into an ellipse and misses the target.

1.1: Drag the satellite dot outward from Earth to change r. Then drag the vertical slider to change v.
1.2: Notice the preview ring: it turns solid teal only when v equals v_circ(r). Away from that value, the ring is dashed.
1.3: The orbit is a circle only for one specific v at each r. That v is v_circ = √(μ/r).

2.1: Each dashed target ring is a circular orbit — its radius is fixed, and Kepler's third law gives its period.
2.2: Set r so the preview ring overlaps the target ring, then tune v until the preview turns teal. The hit registers on LAUNCH.
2.3: Bigger radius → longer period. Rank the targets by period and match each one in turn.

3.1: Read T from the target list. Compute r from T² = (4π²/μ)·r³. Use μ = 4·10⁵ km³/s².
3.2: For T in seconds, r = (μ·T²/4π²)^(1/3). Convert minutes → seconds before you plug in.
3.3: After you have r, don't forget v = √(μ/r). Only circular launches count as hits.
